sentences.sentence: Gabapentin is a prescription medicine used to treat partial seizures , nerve pain from shingles ( postherpetic neuralgia ), and restless legs syndrome (Horizant brand only).
It may also be prescribed off-label for other conditions including diabetic nerve pain, anxiety, and fibromyalgia.
Gabapentin is thought to work by calming overactive nerve signals in the brain and nervous system.
It is an anticonvulsant and nerve pain medication from the drug class gabapentinoids
Gabapentin brand names are Neurontin, Gralise, Horizant, and Relgaabi, which may not be interchangeable.

Gabapentin is not a federally controlled substance, but some states classify it as Schedule V and others require gabapentin prescriptions to be reported to their prescription drug monitoring program (PDMP).
Rules on refills and quantity limits vary by state.
The most common side effects of gabapentin are dizziness, drowsiness (somnolence), and swelling in the hands or feet (peripheral edema).
These often improve as your body adjusts, but do not drive until you know how gabapentin affects you.
Gabapentin works by calming overactive electrical signals in the brain and nervous system.

It does this by binding to the alpha-2-delta subunit of calcium channels in nerve cells, which is thought to normalize chemical signals nerves send to each other and results in a calmer, less excitable nerve circuit.
That same effect helps in different ways depending on what gabapentin is treating:
Epilepsy - dampens the runaway electrical firing that causes seizures.
Postherpetic neuralgia (shingles nerve pain) - reduces the abnormal pain signals from nerves damaged by shingles.
Restless legs syndrome (gabapentin enacarbil / Horizant) - the exact mechanism is less clear, but the same calming effect on overactive nerves is thought to ease the urge-to-move sensation.
Gabapentin is not an opioid, sedative, or anti-inflammatory painkiller.
It works directly on the nerves, which is why it helps nerve-related pain and why it isn't useful for everyday pain like headaches or sprains.
Most people need 1 to 2 weeks of regular dosing for the full effect to build up.
Respiratory depression.

Gabapentin can cause life-threatening breathing problems (respiratory depression) , especially if you already have a breathing disorder (such as COPD), are elderly, or if you use other medicines that can make you drowsy or slow your breathing, such as opioids or CNS depressants.
Seek emergency medical attention if you have very slow breathing.
Suicidal thoughts or behaviors.
Some people have thoughts about suicide while taking and after discontinuing this medicine.
Stay alert to changes in your mood or symptoms.
Tell your doctor right away if you have any sudden changes in mood or behavior, or thoughts about suicide.
Abrupt or rapid discontinuation.
Seizures may occur if you stop using gabapentin suddenly.
Ask your doctor before stopping the medicine.
Stopping abruptly can cause withdrawal symptoms such as anxiety, trouble sleeping, nausea, pain, and sweating.
Sleepiness, sedation, and dizziness.
Avoid driving or participating in hazardous activities until you know how gabapentin will affect you.
Dizziness or drowsiness can cause falls, accidents, or severe injuries.
Brand substitution.
Brands of gabapentin may not be interchangeable.
The most common side effects of gabapentin are dizziness, drowsiness (somnolence), swelling in the hands or feet (peripheral edema), and tiredness.
Other common gabapentin side effects may include:
unsteadiness, poor coordination, or jerky movements
nausea or vomiting
headache
trouble speaking
blurred or double vision
tremor
signs of infection such as fever, chills, or sore throat
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to gabapentin: hives, difficult breathing, or swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat.
Seek medical treatment if you have a serious drug reaction that can affect many parts of your body.
Symptoms may include skin rash, fever, swollen glands, muscle aches, severe weakness, unusual bruising, or yellowing of your skin or eyes.

Tell your doctor right away if you have new or sudden changes in mood or behavior, including new or worse depression or anxiety, panic attacks, trouble sleeping, or if you feel impulsive, irritable, agitated, hostile, aggressive, restless, more active or talkative, or have thoughts about suicide or hurting yourself, while taking this medicine and after stopping it.
Gabapentin can slow or stop your breathing, especially if you have recently used an opioid medicine or alcohol.
A person caring for you should seek emergency medical attention if you have slow breathing with long pauses, blue-colored lips, or if you are hard to wake up.
Some side effects are more likely in children taking gabapentin.
Call your doctor if the child has behavior changes, memory problems, trouble concentrating, or is restless, hostile, or aggressive.
Call your doctor at once if you have:
drowsiness, dizziness, or weakness
problems with balance or muscle movement
increased seizures
This is not a complete list of side effects, and others may occur.
Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects.
You may report side effects to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.
You should not take gabapentin if you are allergic to it.
To make sure this medicine is safe for you, tell your doctor if you have ever had:
breathing problems
diabetes
depression, a mood disorder, or suicidal thoughts or actions
a history of alcohol use or drug addiction
a seizure
(for patients with restless legs syndrome) if you are a day sleeper or work a night shift
kidney disease, or if you are on dialysis
Some people have thoughts about suicide while taking seizure medicine.
Children taking gabapentin may have behavior changes.
Stay alert to changes in your mood or symptoms.
Your family or caregivers should also watch for sudden changes in your behavior.
It is not known if gabapentin will harm an unborn baby.
Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or plan to become pregnant.
Do not start or stop seizure medication during pregnancy without your doctor's advice, because having a seizure during pregnancy could harm both mother and baby.
If you are pregnant, your name may be listed on a pregnancy registry to track the effects of gabapentin on the baby.
Ask a doctor if it is safe to breastfeed while using gabapentin.
Take gabapentin exactly as prescribed by your doctor.
Follow all directions on your prescription label and read all medication guides or instruction sheets.
Your doctor may occasionally change your dose.
Never take gabapentin in larger amounts, or for longer, than prescribed.
Your dose needs may change if you switch to a different brand, strength, or form of this medicine.
Avoid medication errors by using only the medicine your doctor prescribes.
Neurontin can be taken with or without food.
Gralise should be taken with food, with the evening meal.
Swallow Gralise and Horizant tablets whole.
Do not crush, break, chew, or dissolve them.
If you break a scored Neurontin tablet and take only half, take the other half at your next dose, and use it within 28 days.
Measure liquid medicine with the supplied measuring device, not a kitchen spoon.
Doses are based on weight in children.
Your child's dose may change if the child gains or loses weight.
Do not stop taking gabapentin suddenly.
Stopping suddenly may cause increased seizures or withdrawal symptoms.
Follow your doctor's instructions about tapering your dose, usually gradually over at least a week.
This medicine can affect the results of certain medical tests.
Tell any doctor who treats you that you are using gabapentin.
Your kidney function may need to be checked, and your dose may change based on the results.
Store tablets and capsules at room temperature away from moisture and heat.
Store the liquid medicine in the refrigerator; do not freeze.
Follow all storage instructions provided.
Your pharmacist can provide more information about how to store this medicine.
Take gabapentin exactly as prescribed.
Your dose may differ from the ranges shown here.
Patients 12 years and older Dose: starting dose gabapentin 300 mg 3 times a day, which may be titrated up to a maximum dose of 600 mg 3 times a day if needed.
Patients 3 to 11 years of age Dose: the starting dose range is 10 to 15 mg/kg/day, given in 3 divided doses.
The recommended dose in patients 3 to 4 years of age is 40 mg/kg/day, and in patients 5 to 11 years of age is 25 to 35 mg/kg/day, given in 3 divided doses.
The recommended maintenance dose is reached by upward titration over approximately 3 days.
Less than 3 years: Not recommended
Note:
Leave no more than 12 hours between doses
Dose should be adjusted in patients with reduced kidney function.
Your doctor will determine your dose based on your kidney function.
Use: Adjunctive therapy in the treatment of partial onset seizures, with and without secondary generalization, in patients 3 years of age and older.

sentences.section_title: What happens if I miss a dose?
sentences.sentence: Take the medicine as soon as you can, but skip the missed dose if it is almost time for your next dose.

sentences.section_title: What happens if I miss a dose?
sentences.sentence: Do not take two doses at one time.

sentences.section_title: What happens if I miss a dose?
sentences.sentence: If you take Horizant: skip the missed dose and take your next dose at the regular time.

sentences.section_title: What happens if I miss a dose?
sentences.sentence: Do not use two doses at one time.
Seek emergency medical attention or call the Poison Help line at 1-800-222-1222.
An overdose can be fatal.
Overdose symptoms may include slow breathing, double vision, tremor, slurred speech, drowsiness , change in your mental state, dizziness, tiredness, or diarrhea .

sentences.section_title: What should I avoid while taking gabapentin?

sentences.section_title: What other drugs will affect gabapentin?
sentences.sentence: Taking gabapentin with other medicines that make you drowsy or slow your breathing can cause dangerous side effects, including life-threatening breathing problems.

sentences.section_title: What other drugs will affect gabapentin?
sentences.sentence: Ask your doctor before using gabapentin with:

sentences.section_title: What other drugs will affect gabapentin?
sentences.sentence: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking gabapentin, because it can add to these effects.

sentences.section_title: What other drugs will affect gabapentin?
sentences.sentence: Some medicines change the amount of gabapentin in your body:

sentences.section_title: What other drugs will affect gabapentin?
sentences.sentence: Antacids that contain aluminum or magnesium (such as Maalox) can reduce gabapentin absorption.

sentences.section_title: What other drugs will affect gabapentin?
sentences.sentence: Take gabapentin at least 2 hours after an antacid.

sentences.section_title: What other drugs will affect gabapentin?
sentences.sentence: Morphine can increase gabapentin levels, which may increase drowsiness and the risk of breathing problems.

sentences.section_title: What other drugs will affect gabapentin?

sentences.section_title: What other drugs will affect gabapentin?
sentences.sentence: Gabapentin does not usually interact with other seizure medicines, such as phenytoin, carbamazepine, valproic acid, or phenobarbital, because it is not broken down by the liver.
